Names the subjective nature of aerial surveys as the reason accuracy evaluation matters, and records the change in the reported severity metric from killed trees per acre to percent mortality within damage polygons, which is a direct warning about comparing survey years.

title: Evaluating annual spruce budworm defoliation using change detection of vegetation indices calculated from satellite hyperspectral imagery
method: change detection of vegetation indices from satellite hyperspectral imagery against ground-verified annual defoliation
validation_design: ground verification data, scarce by the authors' account
notes: States that current operational annual defoliation estimates come from visual observation from small aircraft, defining broad defoliation classes which are subjective and spatially can be inaccurate. That is the label source this project uses.

title: Discriminant Analysis of the Damage Degree Caused by Pine Shoot Beetle to Yunnan Pine Using UAV-Based Hyperspectral Images
method: one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlation and stepwise discriminant analysis to build a damage-degree diagnostic model
host: Pinus yunnanensis, 80 trees in four plots
validation_design: four sample plots, discriminant model validated internally
notes: Small but fully ground-referenced sample with an explicit damage-degree gradient.

title: An Evaluation of Forest Health Insect and Disease Survey Data and Satellite-Based Remote Sensing Forest Change Detection Methods: Case Studies in the United States
method: three change-detection algorithms on Landsat and MODIS producing forest change products, assessed against TimeSync reference data and compared with the Insect and Disease Survey
sensor: Landsat, MODIS, against Insect and Disease Survey polygons
host: Southern New England and Rio Grande National Forest
validation_design: independent accuracy assessment using TimeSync reference data
notes: CENTRAL FOR RQ4. The operational programme explicitly designed to supplement, not replace, aerial insect and disease survey data, with an independent reference-based accuracy assessment.

title: Time-series approach for mapping mountain pine beetle infestation extent and severity in the U.S. Central Rocky Mountains
method: time-series regression mapping infestation severity as within-pixel percentage, using Landsat, topography and aerial detection survey polygons as covariates
sensor: Landsat, digital elevation model, USFS aerial detection survey polygons
validation_design: validation against a randomly selected subset, reference from interpreted NAIP imagery
accuracy_metric: difference between predicted and reference severity
accuracy_value: no statistical difference between predictions and validation subset, as stated in the abstract
notes: Uses aerial survey polygons as a model covariate rather than as ground truth, which is one way to use an imperfect label source honestly.

title: Detecting Drought-Induced Tree Mortality in Sierra Nevada Forests with Time Series of Satellite Data
method: two-stage random forest trained with forest aerial detection survey data on MODIS index metrics and topographic variables
sensor: MODIS, aerial detection survey data as training labels
notes: Trains directly on aerial survey labels, the same dependency this project has, at coarse support.

title: Forest pests and home values: The importance of accuracy in damage assessment and geocoding of properties
method: matching estimator with Bayesian regression adjustment quantifying the effect of geocoding and damage assessment error on estimated losses
validation_design: comparison of estimates under different error assumptions
accuracy_value: both geocoding and damage assessment errors led to substantial biases
notes: States verbatim that the Forest Service's Aerial Detection Survey is generally too coarse to be informative for property valuation that depends on highly localized spatial data. A blunt independent verdict on survey polygon positional quality.

title: Detecting mistletoe infestation on Silver fir using hyperspectral images
method: hyperspectral image classification of infested versus non-infested fir
agent: white mistletoe (Viscum album), a parasitic plant
notes: Silver fir host with a non-insect biotic agent that produces a physiologically similar water-stress signature to an adelgid, and is therefore a candidate confusing agent.

title: Estimating the Total Economic Impact of Black Bear Peeling in Western Oregon Using GIS and REMI
method: GIS and economic modelling of damage detected in annual aerial forest health surveys
validation_design: landowner survey data as an alternative estimate
accuracy_value: trees that scar over peeling are not detected by aerial surveys, as stated in the abstract
notes: A clean statement of aerial survey omission: damage that heals is invisible to the survey, so the survey systematically undercounts sublethal damage.

title: Aerial mapping canopy damage by the aphid Essigella californica in a Pinus radiata plantation in southern New South Wales: what are the challenges?
method: aerial mapping of canopy damage, with an explicit discussion of the challenges
host: Pinus radiata plantation, southern New South Wales
notes: Identity resolved by title only, abstract not retrieved. Retained because it is the only record in the set on aerial survey mapping of an adelgid-adjacent sap-feeding aphid, whose damage is chronic and diffuse like the adelgid's. Priority full-text read.

title: Identifying Subalpine Fir (Abies lasiocarpa) Attacked by the Balsam Woolly Adelgid (Adelges piceae) Using Spectral Measurements of the Foliage
method: stepwise discriminant analysis on branch-level high spectral resolution foliage measurements, then integration across wavebands to simulate SPOT5-HRVIR
sensor: field spectroscopy at branch level, simulated SPOT5-HRVIR
validation_design: stepwise discriminant analysis, cross-validation not stated in abstract
accuracy_metric: classification accuracy of infested versus non-infested
accuracy_value: 94% with a three-variable model using the red-green index, 670 nm and 1912 nm; 83% with a single-variable model
notes: CENTRAL RECORD FOR RQ1, already cited as Cook 2010. The 94% figure is at branch support under field spectroscopy, not at polygon support from satellite, and the comparison is infested versus non-infested on one host, not adelgid versus a second insect. The abstract also states that aerial surveys are conducted for detection of adelgid infestations, which is the label provenance this project inherits.

title: Mountain Pine Beetle Red-Attack Forest Damage Classification Using Stratified Landsat TM Data in British Columbia, Canada
method: classification of red-attack damage from Landsat TM stratified by GIS forest inventory, trained with field and aerial survey point data
sensor: Landsat TM 1999, aerial and field survey points, GIS forest inventory
host: mature lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta), Fort St James Forest District, British Columbia
validation_design: field and aerial survey point data
notes: British Columbia, aerial survey point data as reference, stratified by the provincial forest inventory. The direct methodological ancestor of what this project proposes, for a different insect.

title: Short‐term effects of moderate severity disturbances on forest canopy structure
method: mixed-effects models with a non-linear time term applied to repeat NEON lidar canopy structure metrics, across six named moderate-severity agents
agent: press disturbances: beech bark disease, hemlock woolly adelgid, emerald ash borer. Pulse disturbances: spring cankerworm moth, spongy moth, ground fire
host: temperate forest of the eastern United States, one host per agent
accuracy_metric: model-estimated change in structural metrics, no classification accuracy
accuracy_value: high intensity press and pulse disturbances both inhibited canopy height growth; low intensity pulse disturbances facilitated it; high intensity pulse disturbances increased canopy complexity over time
notes: CENTRAL RECORD FOR RQ3 AND A NEGATIVE RESULT FOR H1. Six agents including hemlock woolly adelgid, examined structurally from repeat lidar. The abstract states verbatim that while the impact of press disturbances on other dimensions of canopy structure could not be clearly detected, likely because of compensatory growth, the impact of pulse disturbances over time was more readily apparent using multi-temporal LiDAR data. Adelgid damage is a press disturbance, so this is direct published evidence that the structural signal for the agent class of interest is weak. It compares agents rather than classifying them, and each agent sits on a different host. Not in references.bib.

title: Using Remote Sensing and Climate Data to Map the Extent and Severity of Balsam Woolly Adelgid Infestation in Northern Utah, USA
method: comparison of three model families, spectral only, terrain and climate only, and combined, for infestation severity
sensor: moderate-resolution multispectral satellite imagery, terrain and climate data
validation_design: not stated in abstract, mean R squared reported across runs
accuracy_metric: mean R squared and mean RMSE for severity
accuracy_value: spectral only R2mean 0.482 RMSEmean 0.112; terrain and climate R2mean 0.746 RMSEmean 0.078; combined R2mean 0.836 RMSEmean 0.065
notes: CENTRAL RECORD FOR RQ1, already cited as Campbell 2023 and named as this project's exemplar. Its own abstract states the gap verbatim: while the spectral data successfully detected forest degradation, they failed to distinguish between causal agents of change. That sentence is the strongest published statement in the whole set that agent discrimination for this specific insect is unsolved by spectra alone.

title: Spatial Distribution of Chesapeake Bay Riparian Hemlock Forests Threatened by Hemlock Woolly Adelgid
method: thresholding of existing basal area raster layers to identify subwatersheds and riparian buffers with high host density
notes: Host mapping as a precursor to damage mapping, again showing the host-first sequence.

title: Characterizing recent bark beetle-caused tree mortality in the western United States from aerial surveys
method: compilation and analysis of the aerial survey record 1997 to 2018, converting affected area into mortality area, the canopy area of beetle-killed trees
agent: bark beetles (Curculionidae, Scolytinae), by beetle and tree species
accuracy_metric: mortality area and number of killed trees
notes: CENTRAL FOR RQ4. Records that the US Forest Service changed survey approaches during the record, creating challenges for comparison across years, and that affected area overstates impact relative to mortality area. Both problems apply to the British Columbia archive.

title: Subalpine fir mortality in Colorado is associated with stand density, warming climates and interactions among fungal diseases and the western balsam bark beetle
method: two field survey designs, statewide characterisation plots compared against aerial surveys, and stand health monitoring plots measuring biotic and abiotic factors directly
sensor: field survey compared against aerial survey
agent: western balsam bark beetle (Dryocoetes confusus), Armillaria root disease, black stain fungus (Ophiostoma dryocoetidis), spruce beetle (Dendroctonus rufipennis)
host: subalpine fir (Abies lasiocarpa) and Engelmann spruce (Picea engelmannii), Colorado
validation_design: statewide characterisation plots explicitly compared to aerial surveys
accuracy_metric: association between ground-observed and aerially estimated mortality
notes: CENTRAL RECORD FOR THIS PROJECT'S CONFOUNDS. The comparison class in this project, western balsam bark beetle, is shown here to act inside a mortality complex with two fungi and a second beetle on subalpine fir. Its first research question is whether spruce-fir mortality observed at ground level is similar to that estimated through aerial surveys, which is the RQ4 question in the exact host system. Not in references.bib.

title: Ability of Remote Sensing Systems to Detect Bark Beetle Spots in the Southeastern US
method: comparison of Sentinel-2 and MODIS NDVI products for detecting small bark beetle spots
accuracy_value: Sentinel-2 NDVI shows greater potential than MODIS; MODIS resolution prevents deployment given high spatiotemporal heterogeneity
notes: A clean statement that spatial resolution, not algorithm, is the binding constraint in fragmented forest, which is the situation on coastal British Columbia.

title: Monitoring Forest Infestation and Fire Disturbance in the Southern Appalachian Using a Time Series Analysis of Landsat Imagery
method: comparison of tasseled cap indices, NDVI, EVI and a disturbance index in Landsat time series for capturing infestation and fire
host: Tsuga canadensis and Tsuga caroliniana, southern Appalachians
notes: Two agents in one landscape, an insect and a fire, compared through index performance rather than classified against each other.

title: Combined Effects of Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (Adelges tsugae) Infestation and Treatment with Imidacloprid on Eastern Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) Leaf Radiometry
method: leaf-level radiometry under a factorial of adelgid presence or absence and imidacloprid treatment
agent: hemlock woolly adelgid, with an insecticide treatment as a second factor
accuracy_value: adelgid presence changed lower canopy leaf optical properties indicative of reduced photosynthetic potential and efficiency
notes: Locates the adelgid's optical signal in the lower canopy, which is exactly where passive overhead sensors cannot see and where lidar can.

title: The potential to characterize ecological data with terrestrial laser scanning in Harvard Forest, MA
method: review of terrestrial laser scanning applications at a long-term ecological research site, including dual-wavelength instruments
sensor: terrestrial laser scanning, including the Dual-Wavelength Echidna Lidar, with airborne laser scanning and forest census data
agent: not the focus; the site carries hemlock and hemlock woolly adelgid history
support: plot and individual tree, 35 ha ForestGEO plot
notes: The instrument and site context behind the simulated-GEDI adelgid study, so it establishes what structural data exist for the eastern adelgid system.

title: Spring and Autumn Phenological Variability across Environmental Gradients of Great Smoky Mountains National Park, USA
method: MODIS NDVI time series filtered by cover type, topography and disturbance history to isolate phenological variation
agent: disturbance history used as a filter rather than a response
accuracy_value: elevational effects were greatest in spring and more important than site moisture effects
notes: Quantifies how much phenological signal elevation alone produces, which is the background against which any damage anomaly must be measured in mountainous terrain.

title: Ancient and modern colonization of North America by hemlock woolly adelgid, Adelges tsugae (Hemiptera: Adelgidae), an invasive insect from East Asia
method: 14 microsatellites and mitochondrial COI sequencing to reconstruct lineage structure and colonization history
accuracy_value: eight endemic lineages identified, including a western North American lineage with very high microsatellite heterozygosity suggesting ancient asexuality
notes: Not a remote sensing study. Retained for RQ1 because it independently corroborates the western North American adelgid as a distinct endemic lineage, which is the finding that reorganised this project.

title: A 10-Year Assessment of Hemlock Decline in the Catskill Mountain Region of New York State using Hyperspectral Remote Sensing Techniques
method: hyperspectral collections in 2001 and 2012 with concurrent ground truthing, compared against a ten-year field metric survey
host: eastern and Carolina hemlock, Catskill Mountains
validation_design: two hyperspectral epochs with concurrent ground truthing over a ten-year field survey
accuracy_value: fine twig dieback increased from 9% to 15%; live crown ratio decreased from 67% to 56%; healthy hemlock fell from 59% in 2001
notes: Ten-year repeat with matched ground truth. Quantifies how slow and small the adelgid's canopy change is, which bounds what any single-epoch classifier can see.

title: A foundation tree at the precipice: Tsuga canadensis health after the arrival of Adelges tsugae in central New England
method: aerial photograph mapping of hemlock distribution with a 123-stand subsample examining spatial pattern of infestation and impact
agent: hemlock woolly adelgid, since arrival in 1989
accuracy_value: over 86,000 ha of hemlock forest mapped in 5127 stands
notes: Landscape and stand factors influencing spread and impact for the eastern adelgid, at the scale this project works at.

title: Property Value Impacts of Hemlock Woolly Adelgid in Residential Forests
method: hedonic price models on a decade of property transactions with hemlock health measured biannually by image differencing
host: naturally regenerated hemlock stands, West Milford, New Jersey
validation_design: spatial error and fixed-effects panel models
accuracy_value: hemlock decline consistently caused statistically significant reductions in property values
notes: Uses a remote sensing health series as an economic covariate, an example of the downstream use that makes label accuracy consequential.

title: Monitoring Hemlock Forest Health in New Jersey Using Landsat TM Data and Change Detection Techniques
method: regression relating canopy condition to the temporal difference in near infrared over red reflectance between anniversary Landsat dates, predicting four condition classes
sensor: Landsat Thematic Mapper, anniversary dates 1984 and 1994
host: eastern hemlock (Tsuga canadensis), New Jersey Highlands, 1267 km2
support: 90 m diameter ground plot and pixel
validation_design: 105 plots for model development, 50 plots reserved for accuracy assessment
accuracy_value: R2 0.73 between the vegetative index difference and ground-measured hemlock damage
notes: CENTRAL RECORD FOR RQ1. States verbatim that lightly defoliated hemlock canopy did not differ spectrally from healthy hemlock. That is the detection floor for adelgid damage from moderate-resolution optical imagery, established in 1997 and never overturned in this set.

title: Are U.S. national parks in the Upper Midwest acting as refugia? Inside vs. outside park disturbance regimes
method: LandTrendr automated change detection across 1.5 million ha, with agents assigned inside and outside park boundaries
agent: beaver, blowdown, development, fire, flooding, insect or disease, and forest harvest
host: Upper Midwest United States forest, eight national parks
notes: Seven agent classes, one of the widest in the set, yet all insects and all diseases share a single class.

title: Analysis of Unmanned Aerial System-Based CIR Images in Forestry—A New Perspective to Monitor Pest Infestation Levels
method: colour-infrared UAS imagery from a calibrated modified compact camera at crown and branch level
validation_design: two study sites, design not stated in abstract
notes: Early UAS work at the crown and branch level for a stem-boring beetle.

title: Choice of satellite imagery and attribution of changes to disturbance type strongly affects forest carbon balance estimates
method: carbon budget modelling under four remote sensing products, varying spatial resolution, temporal resolution and whether changes were attributed to disturbance type
agent: disturbance types assigned using supplementary data
validation_design: comparison of estimates under different product choices
accuracy_metric: effect of attribution choice on carbon flux estimates
notes: Shows that attributing change to disturbance type materially changes downstream estimates, which is the practical argument for getting agent right.

title: Post-disaster Forest Management and Bark Beetle Outbreak in Tatra National Park, Slovakia
method: GIS mapping from colour-infrared aerial imagery of windstorm damage and subsequent beetle infestation, presented as simple techniques for managers
agent: Alzbeta windstorm 2004 then Ips typographus outbreak in uncleared wood
host: Norway spruce, Tatra National Park, Slovakia
accuracy_value: 12,000 ha of forest damaged by wind, about 165,000 m3 of damaged wood left uncleared
notes: Documents the causal chain from an abiotic event through uncleared material to a biotic outbreak, so the two agents are not independent.

title: Mapping Mountain Pine Beetle Mortality through Growth Trend Analysis of Time-Series Landsat Data
method: forest growth trend analysis combining Landsat temporal trajectories with decision trees to attribute events from segment characteristics
validation_design: validation reported but figures not extracted from abstract
notes: Names the two obstacles plainly, eliminating observational noise and attributing changes quantitatively.
